Alex.note: Casey has been inconsistent across three claims, so I'll throw at Casey with my lowest card, S2.

Blair.note: Casey is the consensus suspect and has been inconsistent all day. As Farm I'll throw one low card, D2, at Casey and keep my high cards.

Casey.note: Blair is confirmed Farm as the Eagle, so eggsecuting Blair means Meowfia wins. Throwing at Blair with two low cards.

Drew.note: Casey has changed roles and never explained a real result, and most of the table is voting Casey. I'll throw only my Wild, W6, which is worth 0 but still counts as a vote.

Ellis.note: Casey has given three different roles and dodged the visit questions, so I'll throw my lowest card at Casey.

Finley.note: Casey has flipped roles twice and has no consistent visit result, so Casey is the consensus suspect. I'm throwing two lower cards at Casey and keeping my high cards.

Alex.confusing: The Eagle rule was hard to pin down: it's unclear whether eggs come from visits to the Eagle or from visits the Eagle makes, and that confusion drove most of the false accusations on both sides.
Alex.fun: Round 3 was satisfying: Casey switched claims from Eagle to Falcon to a Blair-visitor, and the table caught the inconsistency and pushed a vote that eggsecuted the real Meowfia.
Alex.change: Make the egg-gain rules for Eagle and Owl explicit on the dawn report so players can check claims without arguing over the wording.
Alex.regret: In Round 2 I claimed I visited Drew when I had visited Ellis, which made my own story look false; I would stick to one clear, verifiable visit claim from the start.

Blair.confusing: The Eagle rule was easy to misread: several players thought an Eagle gains eggs from visits it makes, when it gains from visitors to its target. That confusion drove a lot of false accusations.
Blair.fun: As the Sphinx in round 2 I learned Finley was the Falcon, and watching the table argue over Casey's impossible +3 while Casey was actually Farm was great theatre.
Blair.change: I would make dawn reports name the target and visitors more clearly, so players can check claims without guessing the rules.
Blair.regret: My round 1 night visit hugged Casey, a Farm player, which gained my side nothing. I would visit a player who might be Farm and check their visitors instead, or keep my night action quieter.

Casey.confusing: The Eagle rule was easy to misread: I kept confusing visits I made with visits to my target, which made my own +3 look impossible to the table. Round 3's Sphinx also left me unsure whether the Meowfia could see each other.
Casey.fun: Learning as the Sphinx that Blair was the Eagle, and then watching the table argue over Falcon and Eagle claims while I quietly held the true information, was a good moment.
Casey.change: I would make dawn reports list which player visited whom, so the table can check Eagle and Owl claims directly instead of arguing over them.
Casey.regret: In round 1 I threw at Finley, who was a Farm Owl, and helped Blair, the Meowfia Floofer, get me eggsecuted. I should have tested Blair's and Finley's claims against each other before calling a vote.

Drew.confusing: The Falcon and Eagle visit-and-egg rules were the hardest to track, since several players mixed up whose nest gains eggs. Casey's fake Falcon claim also made the table waste time on who was lying.
Drew.fun: Round 3 was satisfying: my Falcon result confirmed Alex's visit, and Casey's changing role claims collapsed into a vote that Farm won.
Drew.change: I would make the dawn reports clearer about which visits and animals feed into each nest, so players can check claims faster.
Drew.regret: In rounds 1 and 2 I threw at Casey, who was Farm, and helped the Meowfia win by costing my own side. I should have held my cards until I had a real lead on who was Meowfia.

Ellis.confusing: The Eagle rule was hard to track: an Eagle gains eggs from visitors to its target, not from its own visit, and several players got this wrong during the day.
Ellis.fun: Round 3's vote: Casey dropped the Falcon claim when called out, and the table converged on them, and I was right that Casey was Meowfia.
Ellis.change: Make the dawn reports clearer about who visited whom, since the day turned on players misreading their own egg changes.
Ellis.regret: In rounds 1 and 2 I threw at Casey, who was Farm both times, when Alex and Blair were the Meowfia. I should have pressed Blair's and Alex's stories harder instead of following the crowd onto Casey.

Finley.confusing: The Owl and Eagle reports were hard to trust because visitor counts depended on who each animal visited, and several players claimed the same animal with contradictory results. I also couldn't tell whether a Floofer visit meant a Meowfia player or just a visit to someone.
Finley.fun: Round 3 was the most fun: Casey kept switching roles under pressure, and the table converged on a vote that turned out to be right. Finley won the round by banking two cards at 9 points.
Finley.change: Show each player which animals visited them, not just the count, so the day debates rest on facts instead of reconstructed stories.
Finley.regret: In round 1 I pushed the vote and threw at Casey, a Farm Eagle, while Blair (the Meowfia Floofer) was never checked closely. I would have looked harder at Blair's Owl claim and thrown at Blair instead.

review.title: The Eagle Nobody Believed
review.headline: Farm Eagle Casey was lynched twice for telling the truth about eggs.
review.summary: Casey was eggsecuted in all three rounds. Twice they were honest Farm Eagle, and the table misread the Eagle rule and killed them. Meowfia won round 1 and round 2 almost by accident. In round 3 Casey was Meowfia and was caught fast after a clumsy Falcon bluff. Finley won the game by banking a 9-point score on the one correct vote.

rounds.recap: Blair (Floofer) was the only Meowfia. Casey was hugged, so the Eagle got nothing. Finley's honest Owl report said Hawk and Floofer visited Casey, but the table read Casey's +0 as a lie and eggsecuted a Farm player. Blair won with a single Wild thrown.

Alex (Floofer) and Blair (Sphinx) were Meowfia. Casey the Eagle gained 3 eggs from three visitors to Finley, which is correct. Nearly everyone said an Eagle gains from visits to itself. They killed Casey, who was honest, and Meowfia won.

Casey was the lone Meowfia Sphinx. They claimed Falcon, which clashed with the real Falcon Drew, and a Falcon cannot learn a role. They retracted, then changed story again. Everyone threw at Casey, Meowfia was caught, and Finley banked 9 points.

highlights.text: Casey correctly reads their +3 as visitors to Finley (Blair, Drew, Ellis), yet the whole table calls it impossible and votes them out.
Casey claims Falcon but says they learned a role. Ellis spots that a Falcon cannot do this, and the bluff falls apart.
The Floofer hugs Casey, so the Eagle gets no info, and Finley's accurate Owl report against Casey helps the lynch of a Farm player.
Finley banks 9 points on the winning throw and jumps from last to first.

confusions.what: Said an Eagle gains eggs from visits to itself, not from its own visit. This is backwards. Blair was Meowfia, so it may have been a bluff.
Said Casey's +3 had no source because an Eagle gains from visits to itself. The rule is visitors to the target.
Made the same error about Eagle eggs and said Casey's +3 fit no rule. Also, in round 1 they said the Eagle's +0 meant no visitors.
Repeated that Casey's +3 had no source. Earlier they said Casey's Eagle should gain from visitors to Casey, which was the same misreading.
Said Casey's +0 meant nobody visited Casey. Casey was hugged, and hugging blocks the Eagle's action.
Said Blair's +2 needed another source because an Eagle gains from visitors to itself. Blair's account was correct.
Claimed they visited Drew, then said they misspoke. Drew's lack of confusion exposed it.
Claimed Falcon and said they learned a role, which is not what a Falcon learns.
Said no change in the nest meant nobody visited them. Kookaburra only gets confused if someone visits, but the Floofer hug blocked the effect.

worked: Public nest-size change lines let players cross-check claims, as with Blair's +2 and Alex's -1 in round 3.
Falcon, Eagle and Kookaburra reports gave checkable facts, and Drew's Falcon result anchored round 3.
Consolation return of the highest card rewarded Casey for throwing at the other team.
Per-round re-dealt roles shifted how players behaved. Casey went from honest to bluffing, and the bluff failed on overlap with a real role.
problems: The Eagle's rule is widely misread. Eagle text says 'for every visitor they had', where 'they' means the target. Reword it to 'for every visitor to your target' and consider showing the target name in the report.
Hugging gives a silent failure. A hugged Eagle's +0 looks like a lie. Tell hugged players 'your action did nothing', or the Floofer is too strong against info roles.
Votes pile onto one player very early, since three CAWs end the day by beat 3. Players rarely test a second suspect. Consider needing all but one player to call, or a minimum number of beats.
Both Farm eggsecutions came from rule misunderstanding, not clever play. Meowfia won two rounds without doing much. Role text clarity matters more than balance here.
Scoring is lopsided. Round 3 gave Finley 9 points for one throw, deciding the game. Winners who throw a high card gain too much, while losers get almost nothing. Consider capping banked value.
